title: The Pain of Exclusion Is Real
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Field Note grounds a practical leadership tactic in the psychology of social pain, noting that exclusion from meetings, activities, or decisions registers in the brain much like physical injury and can linger far longer than a physical wound. The author argues this same mechanism applies even to resistant, rule-breaking team members who outwardly claim indifference to the group — they too are wired to avoid social rejection, whether they admit it or not. From there the piece pivots to a counterintuitive last-resort tactic: rather than continuing to chase a disengaged colleague's compliance, a leader can deliberately agree to exclude them from team activities, and the resulting social pain often produces the shift in attitude that direct confrontation could not. The essay frames pain itself, used judiciously, as a legitimate teaching mechanism for stubborn behavioral problems.
points: Social pain from exclusion registers in the same brain regions as physical pain and can linger for days, months, or years — far longer than most physical injuries.
Even team members who claim indifference to the group are still wired to avoid social rejection, whatever they say to the contrary.
As a last resort, deliberately excluding a chronically disengaged team member from activities can produce a sharper shift in attitude than continued confrontation.
The tactic works because it lets social pain, not the leader's argument, do the teaching.
quotes: Whenever people feel abandoned, rejected, or disconfirmed, they experience an intense pain not unlike the physical pain we endure after being injured.
In fact, social and physical pain register in the same area of the brain and share many of the same symptoms.
Unlike the physical pain of an ailment or sprain, social pain can linger long past an incident, sometimes for days, months, and even years.
The truth is, even these wayward and highly resistant colleagues don't want to be excluded, ignored, or rejected by the team and the team leader.
Used as a last resort, leaders who purposely exclude team members will often find a huge shift in their willingness to play along.
The social pain dissipates quickly once it is done teaching resistant colleagues what really matters. Pain is one way we learn.
